Local rankings change with the searcher's location. A plumber can rank first in the map pack near its office and not appear at all three miles away. A single rank check from the city center hides this, so local businesses need geo-grid tracking that checks the same keyword from many points across the service area.

A grid tool drops a pattern of pins, often a 5x5 or 7x7 layout, over your market and records your map-pack position at each one. The result is a heat map that shows where you are strong and where competitors take over. Run it for your main service keywords plus the category term, such as "dentist" or "roofer", and repeat it monthly with the same grid size and spacing so results are comparable.

Use the grid to guide work on your Google Business Profile, reviews, location pages and local links. If you are weak on one side of town, a location page, local citations and reviews from customers in that area can help. Grid results move slowly, so judge changes over a few months rather than week to week.
### Account for device, location and personalization

Rankings differ between mobile and desktop because the layouts, features and sometimes the ordering differ. Google indexes the mobile version of your site, and most local and consumer searches happen on phones. Track mobile as your primary view and desktop as a secondary one unless your buyers clearly use desktop.

Location matters even for non-local keywords. A national query can return different results in different states, and city-level differences are common for service terms. Set your rank tracker to the cities or ZIP codes where your customers are, and avoid checking rankings by searching in your own browser.

Your own searches are shaped by your location, history and signed-in state, so they rarely match what a customer sees. If you must check by hand, use a private window, sign out, and confirm the location setting. Treat manual checks as a sanity test and rely on tools for reporting.
### Track visibility in AI answers

Search now includes AI Overviews in Google and answers from assistants such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Copilot. These do not have a classic position, so you track whether your brand is mentioned, whether your pages are cited as a source, and how you are described. Build a fixed list of prompts that match buyer questions, like "best roofing company in Tampa" or "how much does a kitchen remodel cost".

Run the same prompts on a regular schedule and log mentions, citations, competitors named and the sources each engine used. Answers vary between runs, so run each prompt more than once and look at the share of runs where you appear. Several rank trackers now add AI Overview tracking, and dedicated AI visibility tools cover the chat assistants.

Search Console includes AI Overview and AI Mode traffic inside the normal Performance totals without a separate filter. That means you need your own prompt tracking to see AI visibility directly. Pair it with referral traffic from AI tools in your analytics to see whether mentions turn into visits.
### Compare the main tracking methods

Each method answers a different question, so most businesses use two or three together. The table below summarizes what each one is best for and where it falls short.

A typical setup for a local service business is Search Console for real performance, a rank tracker for 50 to 150 priority keywords, and a monthly grid scan for core map-pack terms. Ecommerce and national sites usually lean more on Search Console and the rank tracker. Add AI visibility tracking once your core pages are in good shape and buyers are likely to ask assistants for recommendations.

| Method | Best for | Limits | Typical cadence |

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Google Search Console | Real impressions, clicks and average position across all queries | Averages hide detail; rare queries are hidden; data lags by a few days | Weekly review, monthly report |

| Rank tracker | Exact positions for a fixed keyword list by device and location | Single sample per check; costs scale with keyword count | Daily or weekly checks |

| Local grid tracker | Map-pack positions across a service area | Only covers local results; grid settings must stay consistent | Monthly |

| AI visibility tracking | Brand mentions and citations in AI Overviews and assistants | Answers vary between runs; no standard position metric | Weekly or monthly |

| Manual checks | Quick sanity tests of a single result | Personalized and not repeatable | As needed |
### What to report and how often

Rankings are a leading indicator, so report them next to the outcomes they should drive. A good monthly SEO report shows organic clicks, impressions, leads or sales from organic search, and ranking movement for priority keyword groups. Explain what changed and why, then list the next actions.

Monthly reporting suits most businesses because rankings fluctuate day to day. Weekly checks are useful for spotting problems early, such as a sudden drop after a site change, but they should stay internal. Quarterly reviews are the right time to judge strategy, since content and links often take months to show their full effect.

Keep the report simple and consistent. Use the same keyword groups, locations and date comparisons each month, and compare against the same period last year where seasonality matters. If you want a baseline before you start tracking, our free SEO audit tool and 40-point audit show what is holding rankings back.

- Organic clicks and conversions, month over month and year over year

- Average position and visibility for priority keyword groups

- Map-pack grid results for core local terms

- AI answer mentions and citations for a fixed prompt set

- Pages gaining and losing traffic, with notes on cause

**Why does my rank tracker show a different position than Search Console?** A rank tracker records one check from one location and device at one moment. Search Console averages your top position across every real impression, from many locations and devices. Both are valid, so use the tracker for controlled trends and Search Console for real-world performance.
**How often should I check my SEO rankings?** Let a tool check daily or weekly so you catch sudden drops, but review and report monthly. Day-to-day movement is mostly noise. Judge strategy changes over a quarter or longer.
**Is average position in Search Console a good KPI?** It is useful as a trend for a page or a group of related queries. It is weak as a sitewide KPI because new rankings for broad terms can lower the average while traffic grows. Pair it with clicks and conversions.
**Can I track rankings for free?** Yes. Search Console is free and covers real Google data for your site. For spot checks of specific keywords you can use our free SEO rank checker, then move to a paid tracker when you need scheduled history.

---

## How to do SEO keyword research
URL: https://www.bestseocompany.us/guides/seo-keyword-research

**Short answer:** To do SEO keyword research, start with the words customers use, expand them with keyword tools, and check search intent by studying the results page. Weigh difficulty against business value, group related terms into clusters, and assign each cluster to one page. Add local modifiers and question keywords so pages can answer searches and AI prompts directly.

- Start from customer language, then use tools to expand and measure it.
- The results page tells you the intent and the content format Google prefers.
- Prioritize by business value and realistic difficulty before volume.
- Map each keyword cluster to a single page to avoid competing with yourself.

### Step 1: Gather seed topics from customers

The best seed keywords come from the people who buy from you. Read sales call notes, support tickets, reviews, emails and chat logs, and write down the exact phrases customers use to describe their problem. Ask your front desk or sales team which questions they hear every week. These phrases often differ from the terms your company uses internally.

List your core services or products, the problems they solve, and the places you serve. Add the questions people ask before buying, such as cost, timing and how to choose a provider. This list of 10 to 30 seed topics becomes the input for every tool you use next.

Check your own data too. Search Console's Queries tab shows searches you already appear for, including terms you never targeted. Site search logs and paid search term reports are also rich sources of real wording.
### Step 2: Expand the list with keyword tools

Run each seed topic through a keyword tool to find variations, related terms and questions. Google Keyword Planner is free with a Google Ads account and gives volume ranges. Third-party tools add estimated volume, difficulty scores, SERP features and the keywords competitors rank for. Google's autocomplete, People Also Ask and related searches are free sources of real phrasing.

Look at competitor domains as well as seed terms. A competitor gap report shows keywords that similar sites rank for and you do not, which is one of the fastest ways to find missing pages. Treat all tool volumes as estimates, since different tools use different data and models.

Export everything into one spreadsheet with columns for keyword, volume, difficulty and current ranking URL if one exists. Remove terms that are irrelevant, such as job searches or free-download queries if you sell a service. A smaller, relevant list is more useful than a huge one.
### Step 3: Identify search intent and analyze the SERP

Search intent is what the searcher wants to get done. Informational searches want an answer, commercial searches compare options, transactional searches want to buy or book, and navigational searches look for a specific brand. A page that does not match the intent will struggle to rank no matter how well it is optimized.

Search each priority keyword and study the first page. Note the page types that rank, such as service pages, blog guides, product pages, directories or videos. Note the SERP features too, including the map pack, People Also Ask, AI Overviews and shopping results. If the top results are all guides, a sales page is unlikely to rank there.

Check what the ranking pages cover and how deep they go. Look at their headings, the questions they answer and whether they come from large brands or small sites like yours. This tells you the format to build and gives a first read on how hard the term will be.

- Informational: "how long does a water heater last"

- Commercial: "best water heater brands"

- Transactional: "water heater installation near me"

- Navigational: a brand name plus "login" or "phone number"
### Step 4: Weigh difficulty against business value

Volume and difficulty scores are a starting point, but business value decides priority. A keyword with low volume and high purchase intent can be worth more than a broad term with large volume and no buyers. Score each keyword on how closely it matches what you sell, from high to low.

Judge difficulty by looking at the real competition. Tool scores mostly reflect the links pointing at ranking pages. Also consider whether the ranking sites are national brands, whether they match intent well, and whether your site already has authority on the topic. A new site should lean toward specific, longer queries it can win sooner.

Combine the two views into a simple priority score. High value and achievable difficulty go first. High value and high difficulty become long-term targets supported by content clusters and links. Low value terms are dropped or saved for later.
### Step 5: Cluster keywords and map them to pages

Group keywords that share the same intent and would be satisfied by the same page. A quick test is to compare the top results for two keywords. If many of the same URLs rank for both, they belong in one cluster and one page. If the results are different, they likely need separate pages.

Assign each cluster a primary keyword, a few secondary variations and one target URL. Mark whether the page exists, needs an update or must be created. This keyword map prevents two of your own pages from competing for the same query and shows content gaps clearly.

Add local modifiers where location affects the results. Service businesses should map city and neighborhood terms, such as "emergency plumber Austin" or "plumber in Round Rock", to the main service page or to genuine location pages with unique content. Avoid near-duplicate city pages that only swap the place name.

| Primary keyword | Secondary keywords | Intent | Target URL | Status | Priority |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| [main term] | [2 to 5 close variants] | [info / commercial / transactional] | [/page-path] | [exists / update / new] | [high / medium / low] |

| [question keyword] | [related questions] | Informational | [/guides/page-path] | [exists / update / new] | [high / medium / low] |

| [service + city] | [service + neighborhood, near me] | Transactional | [/services/page-path] | [exists / update / new] | [high / medium / low] |
### Step 6: Add question keywords for answer engines

Question keywords start with who, what, why, how, when, how much or can I. They show up in People Also Ask and are the kind of queries AI Overviews and chat assistants answer. Collecting them helps you write pages that give a short, direct answer that an engine can quote.

Pull questions from People Also Ask, autocomplete, forums, review sites and your own customer conversations. Place the most important ones as headings on the relevant page and answer each in the first two or three sentences below it. Longer, detailed questions often deserve their own guide.

Track a fixed set of these questions in AI tools over time to see whether your pages are cited. Question-led content also tends to earn links naturally, because other writers reference clear answers.
### Worked example: a fictional local bakery

This is an illustrative example. The business, location and keyword choices are fictional and include no real search data. Imagine Maple Street Bakery, a small bakery in Columbus, Ohio, that sells custom cakes, wedding cakes and daily pastries. Customers often ask about lead time, cake prices and gluten-free options.

Seed topics from the owner and customer emails include custom birthday cakes, wedding cakes, cake tasting, gluten-free cakes and cupcakes for events. Tool expansion adds variants such as "custom cakes near me", "wedding cake bakery Columbus" and "how far in advance to order a wedding cake". A SERP check shows the map pack and local bakery sites for "custom cakes Columbus", while the lead-time question returns guides and People Also Ask boxes.

The bakery maps its clusters to pages. "Custom cakes Columbus" and related terms go to a custom cakes page. Wedding cake terms go to a wedding cakes page with a tasting section. The lead-time and cost questions become a short FAQ guide that links to both service pages. Neighborhood terms, such as German Village or Clintonville, are mentioned naturally on the pages and in the Google Business Profile instead of on thin duplicate pages.

**How many keywords should one page target?** One page should target one primary keyword plus its close variants and related questions. If two keywords return mostly the same results, one page can rank for both. If the results differ, plan separate pages.
**Are keyword volume numbers accurate?** No tool shows exact volume. Keyword Planner uses ranges, and third-party tools use estimates that can differ widely. Use volume to compare keywords against each other and avoid treating it as a traffic forecast.
**How often should I redo keyword research?** Review your keyword map every quarter and do a fuller refresh once a year. Also revisit it when you add services, enter new locations or see new queries appear in Search Console.

---

## What is SEO link building?
URL: https://www.bestseocompany.us/guides/what-is-link-building

**Short answer:** SEO link building is the work of earning links from other websites to yours. Search engines treat relevant links from trusted sites as a signal that your pages are credible and worth ranking. Good link building uses digital PR, useful content, partnerships and local relationships, and avoids paid or manipulative links that break Google's spam policies.

- A backlink is a link from another site to yours, and quality matters more than count.
- The best links come from relevant, trusted sites that real people read.
- Digital PR, resource pages, broken links and local ties are durable tactics.
- Paid links must use rel="sponsored"; buying links that pass PageRank breaks Google's rules.

### What backlinks are and why they matter

A backlink is a clickable link on another website that points to a page on yours. Google was built on the idea that links act like citations, and links remain one of the ways search engines discover pages and judge their importance. A page with relevant links from respected sites has an easier time ranking for competitive terms.

Links also send referral traffic and build brand recognition. A mention in a local news story, an industry association directory or a partner's website puts your business in front of people who already trust that source. AI answer engines also lean on the wider web to decide which brands are credible, so being cited by trusted sources supports AI visibility too.

Links are not the only factor. Content quality, relevance, technical health and user experience still decide whether a page deserves to rank. Links amplify a good page. They rarely rescue a weak one.
### What makes a quality link

A quality link comes from a site that is relevant to your business, has its own real audience and was placed because the content is useful. A link from a respected trade publication or your city's chamber of commerce is worth far more than many links from unrelated blogs. Ask whether the link would still be worth having if search engines did not exist.

Placement and context matter. A link inside the body of a relevant article, with natural anchor text, carries more weight than a link in a footer or a long list of unrelated sites. The anchor text should describe the destination naturally, and it should vary across links instead of repeating one exact-match phrase.

Check the linking site before you pursue it. Look for real traffic, original content, a clear topic and an editorial process. Warning signs include sites that publish on any topic for a fee, pages stuffed with outbound links and domains that exist only to sell placements.

- Relevance: the site covers your industry, location or audience

- Trust: the site has real readers, original content and editorial standards

- Placement: the link sits in the main content with useful context

- Natural anchor text: descriptive and varied, not keyword-stuffed

- Editorial choice: someone decided to link because it helps their readers
### White-hat link building tactics

Digital PR earns links by giving journalists and editors something worth covering. That can be original data from your own business, a useful expert comment, a local survey or a clear guide on a timely topic. Pitch it to writers who cover your field and make it easy for them to quote and link to the source.

Resource page and broken-link building work well in most industries. Many sites keep pages that list helpful tools or guides, and a useful resource of yours can earn a place there. Broken-link building finds dead links on relevant pages, then offers your working page as a replacement, which helps the site owner fix a problem.

Relationships produce the most durable links. Partners, suppliers, manufacturers and trade associations often list the businesses they work with. Local sponsorships of teams, events and charities can earn links from community sites when the sponsorship is real and the link is properly tagged where required. Unlinked mentions are another easy win. Find pages that name your brand without linking and ask the author to add a link.

- Digital PR: original data, expert commentary, newsworthy stories

- Resource pages: get useful guides or tools listed on curated pages

- Broken-link building: replace dead links with your relevant page

- Partnerships: supplier, manufacturer, association and partner listings

- Local sponsorships and events: community sites and local news

- Unlinked mentions: ask sites that already name you to add a link
### What violates Google's spam policies

Google's spam policies describe link spam as links intended to manipulate rankings. That includes buying or selling links that pass PageRank, which covers paying money, giving free products or exchanging services for a followed link. Paid links are allowed for advertising when they are marked so they do not pass ranking credit.

Private blog networks, or PBNs, are groups of sites built or bought to link to a money site. They often use expired domains with thin or recycled content. Google treats them as link schemes, and sites that rely on them risk losing rankings when the network is detected.

Excessive link exchanges, such as "link to me and I'll link to you" arrangements at scale, also count as spam. So do automated links from comment spam, forum profiles and low-quality directories, and large-scale guest posting with keyword-rich anchor text. Google may ignore these links or take manual action against the site, and recovery can take a long time.
### Using rel="sponsored", rel="nofollow" and rel="ugc"

Google supports link attributes that tell it how to treat a link. Use rel="sponsored" for links that are ads, sponsorships or other paid placements. Use rel="ugc" for links inside user-generated content, such as comments and forum posts. Use rel="nofollow" when you do not want to vouch for a link and the other attributes do not fit.

Google treats these attributes as hints, so it may still use the links for discovery. They protect you because they signal that you are not trying to pass ranking credit through a paid or untrusted link. You can combine them, such as rel="sponsored nofollow", if a link fits both cases.

These rules apply to links you receive as well as links you give. If you sponsor an event or pay for a directory listing, the link should carry rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow". Nofollow and sponsored links still bring traffic and brand exposure, so they can be worth having for their direct value.
### Link building tactics compared by effort and quality

Every tactic trades effort against the quality and risk of the links it produces. Use this table to choose a mix that fits your budget and timeline.

Low-effort tactics like unlinked mentions and partner listings are a good place to start because they rely on relationships you already have. Higher-effort tactics like digital PR take more planning but can earn links from sites that are hard to reach any other way. Avoid any tactic in the high-risk row, since cheap links that break the rules can cost you more than they return.

| Tactic | Effort | Typical link quality | Policy risk |

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Digital PR with original data | High | High | Low |

| Unlinked brand mentions | Low | Medium to high | Low |

| Partner and supplier listings | Low | Medium | Low |

| Local sponsorships and events | Medium | Medium | Low if tagged correctly |

| Resource page outreach | Medium | Medium | Low |

| Broken-link building | Medium to high | Medium | Low |

| Paid followed links or PBNs | Low | Low | High, violates spam policies |
### How to measure and run a link building program

Start with a backlink audit. Review the links you already have, the competitors that outrank you and the sites linking to them. Our free backlink checker shows your current link profile, and competitor gaps reveal sites likely to link to businesses like yours.

Set targets around quality and relevance, such as a number of relevant editorial links per quarter. Track referring domains, the pages that receive links, referral traffic and ranking changes for the pages you are supporting. Link building is slow, so judge results over several months.

Point links at pages that deserve them. Strong guides, tools and data pages attract links naturally, and internal links then pass that strength to service pages. If you prefer to hand this off, choose a provider that explains each tactic and refuses to sell links that break Google's rules.

**How many backlinks do I need to rank?** There is no fixed number. It depends on the keyword, the competition and the quality of your content. A few relevant links from trusted sites can matter more than many weak ones.
**Are nofollow links worthless?** No. Google treats nofollow as a hint, and these links still bring referral traffic and brand exposure. A natural link profile includes a mix of followed and nofollow links.
**Is guest posting allowed?** Writing useful articles for relevant sites is fine. Large-scale guest posting done mainly to place keyword-rich links is treated as a link scheme. Write for the audience and keep links natural.
**What should I do about spammy links pointing to my site?** Google usually ignores random low-quality links on its own. Use the disavow tool only if you have a manual action or know of a large set of paid or manipulative links tied to your site.

---

## What is SEO schema for real estate?
URL: https://www.bestseocompany.us/guides/real-estate-schema

**Short answer:** Real estate schema is structured data, usually in JSON-LD, that describes agents, brokerages, listings and events using schema.org types such as RealEstateAgent, Person, SingleFamilyResidence, Offer and Event. Google has no dedicated US listing rich result, so the value lies in clearer entity signals, eligibility for general features like breadcrumbs, and better understanding by AI systems.

- Use JSON-LD and match every property to content visible on the page.
- RealEstateAgent, Person and Organization describe who you are.
- Residence types, Place and Offer describe listings; Event covers open houses.
- Validate with the Rich Results Test and the Schema Markup Validator.

### Structured data basics and JSON-LD

Structured data is code that labels the facts on a page in a format machines read reliably. It uses the schema.org vocabulary, which defines types such as Person, Organization and Place along with properties like name, address and telephone. Search engines use it to understand who a page is about and how the facts relate.

Google supports three formats, and it recommends JSON-LD. JSON-LD sits in a script tag, usually in the page head, and stays separate from the visible HTML. That makes it easier to add through a CMS, a plugin or a template without touching the page layout.

Structured data has to describe content that users can see on the page. If your markup lists a phone number, review rating or price that is not on the page, it is misleading, and Google can ignore it or take manual action. Treat schema as a description of what the page already shows.
### What schema can and cannot do for real estate

Google does not show a dedicated real estate listing rich result in US search. Adding listing markup will not create special property cards with price and photos in organic results. Be wary of anyone who promises that outcome.

The value is in clarity. Schema tells search engines and AI systems that your page belongs to a specific agent or brokerage, where you operate, who your agents are and which property a page describes. That entity clarity helps connect your website with your Google Business Profile, your agent bios and mentions of you around the web.

Schema also makes pages eligible for general features that Google does support, such as breadcrumbs and organization details like your logo. Google narrowed FAQ rich results to a small set of authoritative government and health sites, so FAQ markup rarely produces a visible feature for real estate. It can still help machines read your Q&A content accurately.
### Useful schema.org types for agents and brokerages

Start with the business entity. RealEstateAgent is a subtype of LocalBusiness on schema.org and fits an individual agent's business or a brokerage office. A larger brokerage can use Organization for the company and RealEstateAgent for each office, each with its own address, phone number and hours.

Use Person for individual agents on bio pages. Include name, jobTitle, image, telephone, email and worksFor to link the agent to the brokerage. Add sameAs links to official profiles, such as the agent's license lookup page or professional profiles, so engines can connect the entity across sites.

Use BreadcrumbList on every page with a clear hierarchy, such as Home, Neighborhoods, Riverside, then a listing. Breadcrumbs help Google show a cleaner URL path and help crawlers understand site structure.

| Schema type | Use it for | Key properties |

| --- | --- | --- |

| RealEstateAgent | Agent business or brokerage office | name, address, telephone, url, areaServed, openingHours |

| Organization / LocalBusiness | Parent brokerage or company | name, logo, url, sameAs, contactPoint |

| Person | Individual agent bio pages | name, jobTitle, image, telephone, worksFor, sameAs |

| SingleFamilyResidence / Apartment / Residence | The property on a listing page | name, address, numberOfRooms, floorSize, geo |

| Place | Neighborhood or area pages | name, geo, address, containedInPlace |

| Offer | Sale or rental terms on a listing | price, priceCurrency, availability, businessFunction |

| BreadcrumbList | Site hierarchy on all pages | itemListElement with position, name, item |

| FAQPage | Visible Q&A sections | mainEntity with Question and acceptedAnswer |

| Event | Open houses | name, startDate, endDate, location, organizer |
### Schema for listings, neighborhoods and open houses

For a listing page, describe the property with the most specific residence type that fits. SingleFamilyResidence suits detached homes, Apartment suits a unit, and Residence is the general fallback. Add the address, geo coordinates, number of rooms and floor size as shown on the page.

Describe the sale or rental terms with an Offer that includes price, priceCurrency set to USD and availability. Many sites link the Offer to the property with itemOffered or wrap both in a parent node. Keep prices and status in sync with your listing feed, because stale markup on sold homes sends mixed signals.

Neighborhood and city guide pages can use Place with geo coordinates and a containedInPlace link to the city. Open houses can use Event with a startDate, endDate, location set to the property address and organizer set to the agent. Remove or update the Event once the date passes.
### JSON-LD example for a RealEstateAgent

The example below is for a fictional brokerage office. Replace every value with your own details and make sure each one also appears on the page. Place it inside a script tag with type="application/ld+json".

{"@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": "RealEstateAgent", "name": "Example Realty Group", "url": "https://www.example.com/", "logo": "https://www.example.com/logo.png", "telephone": "+1-555-010-0199", "address": {"@type": "PostalAddress", "streetAddress": "100 Main Street", "addressLocality": "Springfield", "addressRegion": "IL", "postalCode": "62701", "addressCountry": "US"}, "areaServed": ["Springfield", "Chatham"], "openingHours": "Mo-Fr 09:00-18:00", "sameAs": ["https://www.facebook.com/example"]}

This block names the business, gives its contact details and address, lists the areas it serves and links to an official profile. Add a Person block for each agent on their bio page, with worksFor pointing back to this business, and use the same name, address and phone number as your Google Business Profile.
### How to validate your markup

Test every template before you roll it out. Google's Rich Results Test shows whether a page is eligible for Google-supported rich results, such as breadcrumbs, and flags errors in those types. It can test a live URL or a pasted code snippet and renders the page the way Googlebot sees it.

The Schema Markup Validator at validator.schema.org checks all schema.org types, including ones Google does not use for rich results, such as RealEstateAgent and SingleFamilyResidence. Use it to catch syntax errors, misspelled properties and wrong nesting.

After launch, watch the Enhancements reports in Google Search Console for errors across many pages. Spot check listing pages after feed updates, since a template change can break markup on every listing at once.

- Rich Results Test: eligibility for Google features and Googlebot rendering

- Schema Markup Validator: full schema.org syntax and property checks

- Search Console Enhancements: sitewide errors and warnings over time
### Common real estate schema mistakes

The most common problems come from templates and plugins that add markup automatically without anyone checking it. A few small errors repeated across hundreds of listing pages can leave your markup ignored. Review a sample of pages from each template at least once a quarter.

Keep the markup honest and consistent. Your name, address and phone number should match across schema, the page, your Google Business Profile and major directories, which supports the entity clarity that makes schema worth doing.

- Marking up details that are not visible on the page, such as hidden prices

- Adding self-serving review or rating markup for your own business

- Leaving sold or expired listings with active Offer markup

- Using a generic type when a more specific one fits

- Inconsistent business name, address or phone across schema and listings

- Duplicate or conflicting blocks from a theme and a plugin at once

- Expecting a special listing rich result that Google does not offer in the US

**Does schema markup improve real estate rankings?** Schema is not a direct ranking boost. It helps search engines and AI tools understand your business and pages, and it can make pages eligible for features like breadcrumbs. Rankings still depend on content, links, local signals and site quality.
**Should IDX listing pages have schema?** Yes, if the pages are indexable and show unique, accurate listing details. Many IDX setups add basic markup automatically, so test a few pages to see what is there. Avoid adding markup to thin or duplicate listing pages you do not want indexed.
**Which schema type should a solo agent use?** Use RealEstateAgent for the business on the homepage or contact page, and Person on the bio page. Link them with worksFor or by using the same name and details. If you work under a brokerage, reference it as the parent organization.

---

## The Google Business Profile Optimization Checklist for Local Businesses
URL: https://www.bestseocompany.us/blog/google-business-profile-checklist (published 2026-11-18)

**In short:** To optimize a Google Business Profile, use your real business name, choose the most specific primary category, add every service you offer, keep hours accurate, upload real photos regularly, post updates, and ask every happy customer for a review. Avoid keyword-stuffed names, virtual office addresses and frequent edits, which can trigger suspensions or re-verification.

### Start with name, address, phone and categories

Your business name on Google should match what customers see on your sign, truck, invoices and website. Adding keywords or a city to the name breaks Google's guidelines and is a common reason for suspensions. Competitors can also suggest an edit to remove those keywords, which puts your listing under review.

Pick the most specific primary category that describes your core business. A "Water damage restoration service" is more useful than a broad "Contractor" category if that is most of your work. Add secondary categories only for services you actually provide, since every category changes which searches you can appear for.

- Use the legal or trading name you use in the real world.

- Use a local phone number that rings at this location.

- Hide your address if you are a service-area business that does not serve customers at your premises.

- Set service areas by city, county or ZIP code, and keep the list realistic.

- Check competitors' categories in the map pack for ideas you may have missed.
### Fill out services, products and the description

The services section lets you list each job you do, with an optional description and price. Google suggests some services based on your categories, and you can add custom ones in plain language. Write them the way customers search, such as "drain cleaning" or "emergency tooth extraction".

Products work well for businesses with clear packages or popular items, even if you do not sell online. Each product can include a photo, a short description, a price or price range and a link to the matching page on your site. The business description is limited to 750 characters and should explain what you do, who you serve and where, without links or promotional claims.

- List every service, including smaller add-ons that people search for.

- Link products to the most relevant service page on your website.

- Put the most important information in the first sentence of the description.

- Review services after any change to your categories, since Google may reset suggestions.
### Keep hours, attributes and links accurate

Wrong hours frustrate customers and lead to bad reviews. Set regular hours, then add special hours for holidays before they arrive. If you offer after-hours or emergency service, use the extra hours options rather than claiming to be open around the clock when you are not.

Attributes describe things like accessibility, payment options, online appointments and ownership details. Choose the ones that are true and useful to customers. Add your website link, appointment link and any menu or booking links so people can act without leaving Google.

| Profile field | What to check | How often |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Regular hours | Matches your website and phone greeting | Every quarter |

| Special hours | Holidays and planned closures added in advance | Before each holiday |

| Attributes | Only true attributes selected | Twice a year |

| Website and booking links | Links work and point to the right page | Every quarter |

| Service areas | Matches where you actually work | Twice a year |
### Add photos, videos and posts that look real

Photos help customers decide whether to call you. Upload your logo and cover photo, then add real images of your team, vehicles, storefront, finished work and workspace. Avoid stock images, because they tell customers nothing and Google can remove photos that do not represent the business.

Posts let you share offers, updates and events directly on your profile. They are a simple way to show activity and to highlight services that matter to you this season. Aim for a steady rhythm you can keep up, such as one or two posts per week, rather than a burst followed by months of silence.

- Shoot photos on location with your phone in good light.

- Show before-and-after work where it makes sense.

- Add short videos of your team or a job in progress.

- Include a clear call to action button on each post.
### Manage reviews and customer questions

Reviews influence both rankings and conversions. Build a simple routine to ask every customer for a review after a completed job, and reply to every review, good or bad. Short, specific replies that mention the service you performed read better than copied responses.

Google has been scaling back the questions and answers feature on profiles and testing AI-generated answers based on profile content and reviews. That makes complete, accurate profile details more important, because Google draws on them to answer questions. If your profile still shows questions, answer them promptly and correct any wrong answers from the public.
### Avoid verification and suspension pitfalls

Google may ask you to verify by video, phone, text, email or mail, and video verification is now common. Have your signage, tools, vehicle or storefront ready to show on camera, along with proof that you manage the business. Make large edits one at a time, because many changes in a short period can trigger a fresh verification.

Suspensions usually follow a guideline problem. If your profile is suspended, fix the cause first and then file a reinstatement request with supporting documents such as a business license or utility bill. Creating a new profile to get around a suspension usually makes things worse.

- Do not use virtual offices, coworking desks or P.O. boxes as your address.

- Do not create separate profiles for each service you offer.

- Merge or remove duplicate listings for the same location.

- Keep the name, address and phone consistent with your website.

**How many categories should I add to my Google Business Profile?** Add one primary category that matches your core business and only the secondary categories for services you really provide. Google allows several additional categories, but extra categories that do not fit can confuse both Google and customers.
**Do Google Business Profile posts help rankings?** Google does not confirm posts as a direct ranking factor. Posts still help customers see that you are active, promote offers and services, and can improve how many people call or visit after viewing your profile.
**Why did my Google Business Profile get suspended?** Common causes are keywords in the business name, ineligible addresses such as virtual offices, duplicate listings and showing an address for a service-area business. Fix the issue, gather proof of your business, and submit a reinstatement request.

---

## How AI Overviews and AI Search Change Things for Local Service Businesses
URL: https://www.bestseocompany.us/blog/ai-overviews-local-businesses (published 2026-11-18)

**In short:** AI Overviews and AI assistants summarize answers before customers click, so local businesses need content and profiles that AI systems can understand and trust. Keep your Google Business Profile complete, earn steady reviews, publish clear service and FAQ content, use structured data, and get mentioned on reputable local sites. Track calls and leads, since impressions alone tell an incomplete story.

### What changed in local search

Google rolled out AI Overviews in the US in May 2024 and later added AI Mode, a conversational search experience. Both can give a written answer at the top of the results before a searcher scrolls to links. ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and other assistants now answer local questions too.

For a local service business, this changes the early part of the customer journey most. People ask broad research questions like "why is my water heater making noise" or "how much does a crown cost" and often get an answer without visiting a website. When they are ready to hire, they still tend to look at map results, reviews and business profiles.
### Which local searches are most affected

Informational questions are the most likely to trigger an AI answer. Searches with clear hiring intent, such as "emergency plumber near me", still usually show the local pack. The mix shifts over time, so check your own priority keywords in a private browser window every month.

The table below is a rough guide to how different query types behave and where to focus effort. Treat it as a starting point and confirm it against what you see for your own market. Results also differ by city, device and whether the searcher is signed in.

| Query type | Example | What usually shows | Where to focus |

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Research question | why does my AC freeze up | AI answer with cited sources | Helpful FAQ and guide content |

| Cost question | average cost of a root canal | AI answer, sometimes with local results | Honest pricing ranges on service pages |

| Comparison | best family dentist in Tampa | AI answer, local pack and review sites | Reviews and third-party mentions |

| Hiring intent | emergency electrician near me | Local pack and map results | Google Business Profile and reviews |
### Make your business easy for AI to understand

AI systems summarize what they can find and verify. If your website is vague about what you do and where, the AI has less to work with. Spell out your services, service areas, hours, licenses and credentials in plain text on your site and on your Google Business Profile.

Consistency matters as much as completeness. When your name, address, phone and services match across your website, Google, Bing, Apple and major directories, AI tools are less likely to repeat wrong details. Structured data adds another clear signal about who you are.

- Write one focused page per core service and per main location.

- Answer real customer questions in short, direct paragraphs.

- Add LocalBusiness schema with accurate hours, phone and areaServed.

- Keep your Google Business Profile services and description current.

- Correct wrong information on directories and data aggregators.
### Earn trust signals AI tools rely on

AI answers about "the best" local providers often lean on reviews, local news, industry directories and community sites. A steady flow of genuine reviews gives both Google and AI tools more to work with. Specific reviews that mention the service and the town are especially useful.

Third-party mentions also help. Sponsorships, local press, chamber listings, professional associations and partner pages all create references to your business outside your own site. These are the same signals that support traditional local SEO, which keeps the work efficient.
### Adjust how you measure results

When AI answers appear, some searchers get what they need without clicking. Your impressions may rise while clicks stay flat. That can look worrying in a traffic report even when leads are steady.

Track the outcomes that pay the bills. Use call tracking, form tracking and booking data, and look at Google Business Profile calls, direction requests and website clicks. Ask new customers how they found you, and add "AI assistant" as an answer option.

- Phone calls from your profile and website.

- Form submissions and online bookings.

- Branded search volume over time.

- Mentions of your business in AI answers for priority questions.
### A practical 90-day plan

Start with the profile and the pages closest to revenue, then build outward. Each step below supports both map rankings and AI visibility, so nothing is wasted if AI features change again. Review progress at the end of each month.

Do not chase every new AI feature with separate tactics. The businesses that hold up best are the ones with accurate data, strong reviews and genuinely useful pages. That foundation tends to carry over from one search format to the next.

- Month one: audit and complete your Google Business Profile, fix citation errors and add schema.

- Month two: rewrite core service pages and add FAQ sections based on real customer questions.

- Month three: build a review request routine and pursue a few local mentions.

**Do AI Overviews show for local searches?** They can, especially for informational and cost questions. Searches with clear hiring intent, such as "plumber near me", still commonly show the local pack and map results, though Google continues to test different layouts.
**Can I pay to appear in AI Overviews?** There is no organic placement you can buy in AI Overviews. Google has tested ads in and around AI answers, but organic inclusion depends on having clear, trustworthy information the system can find and cite.
**Should a small local business invest in AEO or GEO?** For most local businesses, AEO and GEO build on the same foundation as local SEO. Complete profiles, consistent listings, reviews and clear service pages help in both. Specialist work makes sense once that foundation is solid.

---

## Core Web Vitals in Plain English, With a Focus on INP
URL: https://www.bestseocompany.us/blog/core-web-vitals-inp (published 2026-11-18)

**In short:** Core Web Vitals are three Google metrics for real user experience. LCP measures loading, INP measures how quickly a page responds to taps and clicks, and CLS measures visual stability. INP replaced FID in March 2024. A good INP is 200 milliseconds or less. Check field data in PageSpeed Insights and Search Console, then reduce heavy JavaScript.

### What Core Web Vitals measure

Core Web Vitals are part of Google's page experience signals. They try to capture how a page feels to a real visitor. Each metric has a "good", "needs improvement" and "poor" range, and Google assesses them at the 75th percentile of visits.

Good scores alone will not make a weak page rank. They work more like a baseline for user experience, and they matter most when competing pages are similar in relevance. They also affect conversions, because slow or jumpy pages lose visitors.

| Metric | What it measures | Good | Poor |

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) | How fast the main content appears | 2.5 seconds or less | Over 4 seconds |

| INP (Interaction to Next Paint) | How fast the page responds to input | 200 ms or less | Over 500 ms |

| CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) | How much the layout jumps around | 0.1 or less | Over 0.25 |
### INP explained

Interaction to Next Paint measures the delay between a user action and the next visual update on screen. Actions include clicks, taps and key presses. The page records interactions during the visit and reports a value close to the slowest one.

INP replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. FID only measured the delay before the browser began handling the first interaction. INP covers the full response time for interactions throughout the visit, so it catches sluggish menus, filters and forms that FID missed.

- Input delay is the time spent waiting for the main thread to be free.

- Processing time is how long your event handlers take to run.

- Presentation delay is the time to calculate layout and paint the update.
### How to measure in PageSpeed Insights and Search Console

PageSpeed Insights shows two kinds of data. The top section shows field data from the Chrome User Experience Report when enough real visits exist. The lower Lighthouse section is a lab test, which cannot measure INP directly and uses Total Blocking Time as a rough stand-in.

Search Console's Core Web Vitals report groups similar URLs and shows which groups are good, need improvement or are poor. It uses the same field data, collected over a rolling 28-day window. After you fix an issue, you can start validation in the report and watch it update as new data arrives.

- Use PageSpeed Insights to check a single important URL.

- Use Search Console to find patterns across templates.

- Use Chrome DevTools Performance panel to find slow interactions on your own device.

- Add the web-vitals JavaScript library if you want your own real-user data.
### Common INP fixes

Most INP problems trace back to JavaScript blocking the main thread. Third-party scripts such as chat widgets, tag managers, ad scripts and heatmap tools are frequent causes. Large single-page app bundles and heavy page builder themes are others.

Start by removing what you do not need, then make the rest do less work at once. Break long tasks into smaller pieces so the browser can respond between them. Show immediate visual feedback when a user clicks, even if the full result takes a moment longer.

- Audit third-party scripts and remove unused ones.

- Load non-critical scripts with defer or after user interaction.

- Split long tasks and yield to the main thread.

- Avoid large DOM sizes, especially on mobile.

- Debounce input handlers on search boxes and filters.
### Quick wins for LCP and CLS

LCP is usually limited by a large hero image, slow server response or render-blocking resources. Compress and properly size the hero image, serve modern formats like WebP or AVIF, and do not lazy-load the main image. A CDN and good caching often help server response time.

CLS comes from content that moves after it first appears. Set width and height on images and video, reserve space for ads and embeds, and avoid inserting banners above existing content. Web fonts can also cause shifts, so use font-display settings and preload key fonts.
### Where to start on a small business site

Focus on the templates that bring in leads, such as the home page, service pages and location pages. Fix issues at the template level so one change improves many URLs. Retest on a mid-range phone on mobile data, since that is closer to what many visitors use.

If your site runs on WordPress or a page builder, check plugins first. Each plugin can add scripts and styles to every page. Removing a few unused plugins and switching to a lighter theme often improves all three metrics at once.

- Check Search Console to see which page groups fail.

- Fix the slowest lead-generating template first.

- Remove or delay third-party scripts that are not essential.

- Retest after each change so you know what helped.

**When did INP replace FID?** Google made Interaction to Next Paint a Core Web Vital in March 2024, replacing First Input Delay. FID was then retired from Search Console and other Google tools.
**Why does PageSpeed Insights show no INP data for my page?** INP needs field data from real Chrome users. If a page or site has too little traffic, the Chrome User Experience Report has no data to show. Lab tests use Total Blocking Time as a rough proxy instead.
**Will passing Core Web Vitals improve my rankings?** It can help at the margins, especially against similar competitors, but relevance and content quality matter much more. Passing scores mainly improve user experience and conversions.

---

## How to Write Service Pages That Rank and Convert
URL: https://www.bestseocompany.us/blog/service-pages-that-rank (published 2026-11-18)

**In short:** A service page that ranks and converts targets one service, matches what searchers want, and makes the next step obvious. Lead with a clear headline and summary, explain the service and process, show proof such as reviews and credentials, answer common questions, and link to related services and locations. Keep the phone number and booking option visible throughout.

### One service, one page

A single page listing every service you offer rarely ranks well for any of them. Google needs a clear page to match each search, and customers want to see that you do the exact job they need. Give each core service a dedicated page with its own title, headline and content.

Group closely related tasks on one page when customers treat them as the same thing. "Water heater repair" and "water heater replacement" may deserve separate pages, while small variations of the same task usually do not. Look at what already ranks for each phrase to decide. If the top results are separate pages for each task, that is a strong hint to split yours too.
### Match search intent

Most service searches come from people ready to hire, compare or get a quote. They want to know whether you do the job, where you work, how soon you can come and roughly what it costs. Answer those questions near the top of the page.

Search the target phrase yourself and study the top results. If they are all local service pages, write a service page. If they are long guides, you may need a supporting article that links to your service page.

| Searcher question | Where to answer it on the page |

| --- | --- |

| Do you do this job? | Headline and first paragraph |

| Do you serve my area? | Summary near the top and a service area section |

| Can I trust you? | Reviews, licenses, photos and guarantees |

| What will it cost? | Pricing range or factors that affect price |

| How do I book? | Call button and form above the fold and repeated below |
### A page structure that works

A predictable structure makes the page easy to scan and easy for search engines to understand. Use one H1 that names the service and, where useful, the main city. Break the rest into short sections with descriptive H2s.

Write in plain language and keep paragraphs short. Explain what the service includes, how the job works and what happens after. Avoid padding the page with generic text just to hit a word count.

- H1 with the service and location.

- Two or three sentence summary with a call to action.

- What is included and signs you need the service.

- Your process, step by step.

- Pricing guidance and financing options if relevant.

- Reviews and proof.

- FAQs and a final call to action.
### Add proof that earns trust

Proof is what turns a visitor into a lead. Show reviews that mention this specific service, photos of real jobs, licenses, insurance, certifications and warranties. Short case examples that describe the problem, the fix and the outcome work well, as long as they are true.

Proof also supports quality signals that Google looks for. Showing who does the work and why they are qualified helps demonstrate experience and expertise. Add a short author or team note on pages that give advice.

- Reviews that mention this service by name.

- Photos of real jobs, ideally before and after.

- License numbers, insurance and certifications.

- Warranties or guarantees in plain language.

- Years in business and team credentials, if they are accurate.
### Use FAQs and internal links

FAQs let you answer objections and long-tail questions without cluttering the main copy. Pull them from real calls, emails and reviews. Keep answers short and direct so they are easy for search engines and AI tools to quote.

Internal links help Google understand how your pages relate. Link from the service page to related services, relevant location pages and helpful articles. Link back to the service page from blog posts and the home page with descriptive anchor text.

- Add three to six FAQs per service page.

- Use FAQ structured data only where it matches visible content.

- Link to two or three related services.

- Link from relevant blog posts using the service name as anchor text.
### Show location relevance without spam

For local businesses, the service page should make your service area clear. Mention the main city and nearby areas naturally, embed a map if useful, and show reviews from local customers. Keep your name, address and phone consistent with your Google Business Profile.

If you serve several cities, create location pages only when you have something unique to say about each one. Copying the same page and swapping the city name creates thin content. Local projects, local team members and area-specific details make each page worth indexing.

**How long should a service page be?** Long enough to answer the questions customers ask before hiring. For many services that is several hundred to over a thousand words, but clarity matters more than length. Compare the depth of pages that already rank.
**Should I put prices on service pages?** If you can, give a range or explain the factors that affect price. Customers search for costs, and a clear answer builds trust. You can still ask for a quote for the exact job.
**Do I need separate pages for each city I serve?** Only if you can make each page genuinely useful with local details, projects or reviews. A strong service page plus a clear service area section is often better than many thin city pages.

---

## How to Get More Google Reviews Without Breaking the Rules
URL: https://www.bestseocompany.us/blog/get-more-google-reviews (published 2026-11-18)

**In short:** To get more Google reviews, ask every customer at the moment they are happiest, make it easy with a direct review link, and follow up once. Do not offer incentives, filter out unhappy customers before asking, or post fake reviews. Google prohibits these practices, and the FTC rule on fake reviews took effect in October 2024. Respond to every review.

### Why reviews matter for local businesses

Reviews are one of the clearest signals of trust for both customers and Google. Google lists prominence, which includes review count and rating, among the factors for local ranking. Customers also read reviews to decide which business to call.

Volume, recency and detail all matter. A steady flow of reviews looks more natural than a sudden burst. Detailed reviews that mention a service and a town also give customers and search engines more context.
### The rules you must follow

Google's policies prohibit fake engagement, including reviews written by the business, its staff or paid third parties. They also prohibit offering anything of value in exchange for reviews and discouraging or selectively soliciting reviews. Breaking these rules can lead to removed reviews, profile warnings or restrictions.

The Federal Trade Commission's final rule on consumer reviews and testimonials took effect in October 2024. It bans fake reviews, buying positive or negative reviews, undisclosed insider reviews and using threats to suppress negative reviews. The FTC can seek civil penalties for knowing violations.

| Practice | Allowed? | Why |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Asking every customer for an honest review | Yes | Fair and representative |

| Sending a direct review link by text or email | Yes | Makes it easy to leave a review |

| Only asking customers who said they were happy | No | Review gating is against Google policy |

| Offering a discount for a review | No | Google prohibits incentives |

| Staff or family writing reviews | No | Conflict of interest and FTC concern |

| Buying reviews from a service | No | Fake reviews are banned under the FTC rule |
### Ask at the right moment

Timing has a big effect on whether people follow through. The best moment is right after a visible win, such as a finished job, a solved problem or a thank-you from the customer. Ask in person first, then send the link while the experience is fresh.

Make it personal and simple. Use the customer's name, mention the job and include a one-tap link to your review form. One polite reminder a few days later is fine, but repeated nagging is not.

- Get your direct review link from your Google Business Profile.

- Turn it into a QR code for invoices, receipts and counter cards.

- Train staff to ask at the end of every job or visit.

- Automate a text or email through your CRM or booking software.

- Track requests and reviews by team member to build the habit.
### Respond to every review

Replies show customers that you care and that real people run the business. Thank positive reviewers and mention the service where it fits naturally. Keep replies short and avoid copying the same text every time.

Negative reviews deserve a calm, professional response. Acknowledge the concern, avoid arguing in public and invite the customer to continue the conversation offline. If a review breaks Google's policies, such as spam or a conflict of interest, report it through your profile, but do not expect removal just because it is negative.
### Extra care for healthcare providers

Doctors, dentists, therapists and other covered entities must protect patient information under HIPAA. A review response that confirms someone is a patient, or mentions their treatment, can disclose protected health information even if the patient shared it first. Keep responses general.

Ask for reviews in a way that respects privacy as well. Do not include treatment details in review request messages. Check with your compliance advisor about your process.

- Never confirm or deny that the reviewer is a patient.

- Do not mention appointments, procedures or conditions.

- Use a general statement and invite them to call the office.
### Build a simple review system

Most businesses do not lack happy customers. They lack a consistent habit of asking. A simple system turns review requests into part of the normal job instead of something staff remember now and then.

Decide who asks, when they ask and how the link is sent. Write a short script for in-person requests and a template for texts and emails. Review the numbers each month and thank the team members who ask most often.

- Add a review request step to your job completion checklist.

- Send the link within a day of the visit.

- Send one reminder only, a few days later.

- Share new reviews with the team to keep the habit going.

**Can I offer a discount in exchange for a Google review?** No. Google's policies prohibit offering money, discounts, free products or any other incentive for reviews. This applies even if you do not ask for a positive review.
**What is review gating?** Review gating means screening customers first, for example with a satisfaction survey, and only sending happy customers to Google. Google prohibits selectively soliciting positive reviews, so ask every customer the same way.
**Can I get a bad review removed?** Only if it breaks Google's policies, such as spam, off-topic content, harassment or a conflict of interest. You can report it from your profile. Honest negative reviews usually stay, so a thoughtful reply is your best tool.

---

## Local Citations and NAP Consistency: What Still Matters
URL: https://www.bestseocompany.us/blog/local-citations-guide (published 2026-11-18)

**In short:** Local citations are online mentions of your business name, address and phone number. Their value today comes from accuracy on the platforms that matter. Claim and correct your Google, Apple, Bing and Yelp listings, submit to the main data aggregators, add key industry directories, and merge or remove duplicates so every source shows the same details.

### What citations do today

A citation is any online mention of your business name, address and phone number, often called NAP. Years ago, building hundreds of directory listings was a common local SEO tactic. Today, more listings rarely move rankings on their own.

Citations still matter for accuracy and trust. Google, Apple, AI assistants and navigation apps pull business data from many sources. When those sources agree, your details are more likely to appear correctly wherever customers look.
### Which platforms matter most

Start with the platforms customers actually use and the sources that feed other services. Then add a small number of industry and local directories that are relevant to your field. Skip low-quality directories that exist only to sell listings.

Apple Business Connect lets you manage how your business appears in Apple Maps, Siri and other Apple apps. Bing Places powers Bing search and maps and can import data from your Google Business Profile. Both take little time to set up.

| Type | Examples | Why it matters |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Core platforms | Google Business Profile, Apple Business Connect, Bing Places | Where most map and local searches happen |

| Review sites | Yelp, Facebook, BBB | Customer research and trust |

| Data aggregators | Data Axle, Foursquare, Localeze | Feed data to many apps and directories |

| Industry directories | Healthgrades, Avvo, Houzz, Angi | Relevant to customers in your field |

| Local sources | Chamber of commerce, local news, associations | Local relevance and real referrals |
### Keep NAP consistent

Choose one official version of your name, address and phone number and use it everywhere. Minor formatting differences such as "St." versus "Street" are usually fine. Different phone numbers, old addresses or outdated business names cause real problems.

Watch out for tracking numbers. If you use call tracking on your website, keep your main local number as the primary number on listings and add the tracking number as an additional phone where the platform allows it. This keeps your data consistent while still measuring calls.

- Use the same business name as your signage and Google profile.

- Format the address the way the USPS recognizes it.

- Use one primary local phone number.

- Keep your website URL consistent, including https and www.
### Find and clean up duplicates

Duplicate listings appear after moves, rebrands, phone changes or when someone creates a listing by mistake. They split reviews, show old information and can confuse search engines. Search each major platform for your business name, phone number and old addresses to find them.

On Google, request a merge or mark a duplicate as closed or nonexistent through the profile tools or support. On other platforms, claim the duplicate and request removal or a merge. Fix the data aggregators too, or old details may come back.

- Search by old phone numbers and previous addresses.

- Check for listings under former business names.

- Look for separate listings created for individual practitioners.

- Document each fix so you can recheck it later.
### A simple citation audit process

Start by writing down your official business details in one document. Include the name, address, phone, website, hours and categories. Everyone who touches your listings should use this as the single source of truth.

Next, check each core platform, aggregator and industry directory against that document. Record the listing URL, whether you have claimed it and any errors you find. Fix the most visible platforms first, then work down the list.

Repeat the audit after any move, phone change or rebrand. These events cause most citation problems, and old details can linger for months. A short checklist makes the next audit much faster.

- Create a master record of your business details.

- List every listing you find in a spreadsheet.

- Claim unclaimed listings where you can.

- Correct errors, starting with Google, Apple, Bing and Yelp.

- Set a reminder to recheck twice a year.
### Should you use a listings service?

Paid listing management tools can push updates to many directories at once. They save time for multi-location brands and businesses that change details often. Some remove your data or revert changes if you cancel, so read the terms.

For a single-location business, manual updates on the core platforms and aggregators are often enough. Recheck the important listings twice a year and whenever your details change. A small amount of regular upkeep prevents most problems.

**Do local citations still help rankings?** Accurate citations on major platforms support local SEO, but adding many low-quality listings rarely moves rankings now. Focus on consistency, core platforms and a few relevant industry sources.
**What are data aggregators?** Data aggregators collect business information and share it with apps, directories, navigation systems and search engines. In the US, examples include Data Axle, Foursquare and Localeze. Correcting data there can fix errors on many downstream sites.
**How do I fix a duplicate Google Business Profile?** If you manage both, remove the extra one or contact support to merge them. If you do not own the duplicate, use the suggest an edit option to mark it as a duplicate or closed. Keep proof of your correct details ready.

---

## Schema Markup for Local Businesses: A Practical Guide
URL: https://www.bestseocompany.us/blog/local-business-schema (published 2026-11-18)

**In short:** Local business schema is structured data, usually in JSON-LD, that describes your business to search engines. Use the most specific LocalBusiness subtype, include name and address, then add telephone, url, opening hours, geo coordinates, sameAs links and areaServed for service-area businesses. Make sure it matches visible page content, then validate it with Google's Rich Results Test.

### What LocalBusiness schema does

Schema markup is code that labels facts on your page so machines can read them. LocalBusiness schema describes your business name, address, phone, hours and more. It helps Google, Bing and AI tools connect your website with your business entity.

Schema does not guarantee a rich result or a ranking boost. It removes ambiguity and supports eligibility for some search features. Google recommends JSON-LD, which sits in a script tag and does not change how the page looks.
### Choose the right subtype

Schema.org has many subtypes of LocalBusiness. Using the most specific one gives a clearer signal about what you do. If no subtype fits exactly, use the closest parent type.

Some subtypes sit under more than one branch. Dentist, for example, is both a LocalBusiness and a MedicalOrganization type. Check schema.org for the full list before you choose.

| Business | Schema type |

| --- | --- |

| Plumber | Plumber |

| Electrician | Electrician |

| HVAC company | HVACBusiness |

| Roofing company | RoofingContractor |

| Dental practice | Dentist |

| Law firm | LegalService or Attorney |

| Real estate office | RealEstateAgent |
### Required and recommended properties

Google's local business documentation lists name and address as required. Recommended properties include telephone, url, geo, openingHoursSpecification, priceRange and aggregateRating where appropriate. Fill in as many as you can support with accurate, visible information.

Keep in mind that Google does not show review stars for a business based on reviews it publishes about itself. You can still mark up genuine reviews on pages where they appear. Just do not expect star snippets from self-serving reviews on your own site.

- name: your real business name.

- address: a PostalAddress with street, city, state and ZIP.

- telephone: your main local number.

- url: the page for this location.

- geo: latitude and longitude of the location.

- openingHoursSpecification: days and hours you are open.

- image and logo: real photos and your logo.
### sameAs, hours and areaServed

The sameAs property lists URLs of your official profiles elsewhere, such as Facebook, LinkedIn, Yelp and your Google Business Profile. It helps search engines confirm that these profiles belong to the same entity. Only include profiles you control.

Use openingHoursSpecification for structured hours, including separate entries for different days. Service-area businesses that do not serve customers at their address can use areaServed to list the cities, counties or regions they cover. Keep the area consistent with your Google Business Profile.
### A short JSON-LD example

Here is a minimal example for a plumber. Replace every value with your own details. Place the code in a script tag with type application/ld+json. {"@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": "Plumber", "name": "Example Plumbing Co.", "url": "https://www.example.com/", "telephone": "+1-555-555-0100", "address": {"@type": "PostalAddress", "streetAddress": "123 Main St", "addressLocality": "Austin", "addressRegion": "TX", "postalCode": "78701", "addressCountry": "US"}, "openingHoursSpecification": [{"@type": "OpeningHoursSpecification", "dayOfWeek": ["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday"], "opens": "08:00", "closes": "17:00"}], "areaServed": ["Austin", "Round Rock", "Cedar Park"], "sameAs": ["https://www.facebook.com/exampleplumbing"]}

For multiple locations, give each location page its own block with that location's details. Link each one to the main brand with the parentOrganization property. Do not put every location's address on every page.
### Validate and maintain

Test every template with Google's Rich Results Test and the Schema Markup Validator at validator.schema.org. Fix errors first, then review warnings to see which ones are worth addressing. Recheck after site updates, since theme or plugin changes can break markup.

Make sure structured data matches the visible page. If your hours change on the page and your Google profile, update the schema too. Markup that contradicts the page can be ignored or treated as spam.

- Run the Rich Results Test on each template.

- Check the Enhancements reports in Search Console.

- Update schema whenever hours, phone or address change.

- Avoid marking up content that visitors cannot see.
### Common schema mistakes to avoid

Most schema problems come from templates and plugins that add markup automatically. Two plugins can output conflicting blocks for the same business. Old hours or phone numbers can also sit in markup long after the page was updated.

Another common issue is using the wrong type or the wrong page. A generic Organization block on every page is fine, but LocalBusiness details belong on the page that describes that location. Review your markup in the page source to see what is actually being output.

- Duplicate or conflicting LocalBusiness blocks from several plugins.

- Hours or phone numbers that differ from the visible page.

- Marking up reviews that are not shown on the page.

- Using a vague type when a specific subtype exists.

- Listing every location's address on a single page.

**Is LocalBusiness schema a ranking factor?** Google has not described it as a direct ranking factor. It helps search engines understand your business and can support eligibility for some search features, which makes it worth adding.
**Should service-area businesses include an address in schema?** Include your address if it is public and matches your Google profile. If you hide your address, use areaServed to describe where you work and keep the markup consistent with what your site shows.
**Where should I put local business schema?** Put it on the home page for a single-location business, or on each location page for multi-location businesses. Use JSON-LD in the page head or body.

---

## The Website Redesign and Migration SEO Checklist
URL: https://www.bestseocompany.us/blog/seo-site-migration-checklist (published 2026-11-18)

**In short:** A safe SEO migration starts with a full crawl and a URL map that sends every old page to its closest new page with a 301 redirect. Keep staging blocked from search engines, check canonicals and internal links, submit new sitemaps, and use Search Console's Change of Address tool when moving domains. Monitor traffic, errors and rankings for several months.

### Before you start: benchmark and crawl

Record where you stand before anything changes. Export organic traffic by landing page, top queries from Search Console and key conversion data. Note rankings for your most important keywords and save copies of current sitemaps.

Crawl the existing site with a tool such as Screaming Frog or Sitebulb. Combine that list with URLs from Search Console, analytics and backlink tools, since crawls miss orphaned pages. This full list becomes the base of your redirect map.

- Export landing page traffic for at least the last 12 months.

- List pages with external backlinks.

- Save current titles, meta descriptions and headings.

- Record current Core Web Vitals and index coverage.
### Map every URL

Build a spreadsheet with each old URL and its new destination. Match pages one to one wherever possible, using the closest equivalent content. Redirecting everything to the home page wastes the value of old pages and confuses users.

Keep URLs the same where you can, since unchanged URLs need no redirect. If a page is being removed with no replacement, decide whether it should redirect to a close parent page or return a 404 or 410. Get sign-off on the map before development finishes.

| Old URL situation | Action |

| --- | --- |

| Same content, new URL | 301 to the new URL |

| Content merged into another page | 301 to the merged page |

| Page removed, close alternative exists | 301 to the closest alternative |

| Page removed, no alternative | Return 404 or 410 |

| URL unchanged | No redirect needed |
### Set up staging safely
